title: Preventing Kitchen Drain Blockages: Understanding FOG Accumulation
description: Warm fats, oils, and grease (FOG) pour smoothly when hot, but as they travel into cool underground or in-wall drainage pipes, they rapidly cool and solidify against the pipe walls. Over time, this waxy layer thickens, catching passing food particles and gradually choking off water flow. Running hot water down the drain only relocates the grease further down the line where it eventually cools anyway. To protect your drainage system, scrape cookware into the waste bin and wipe heavy grease with paper towels before washing. How do you handle leftover cooking oils in your home or shop?

The cross-section clearly reveals the inside of a white PVC drain pipe where a thick, realistic yellow-white layer of solidified grease and fat lines the bottom and sides of the internal pipe wall, significantly reducing the internal diameter for water flow. Clean, bright studio lighting highlights the contrast between the clean upper pipe and the constricted lower channel. Soft neutral background, realistic plumbing fittings and wall connection. Space left clean at the top and bottom for visual balance. Photorealistic textures, no text, no labels, no arrows, no logos, no watermarks, no fake branding.
visual_story: The visual uses a clear pipe cross-section to show what happens inside a drain when warm grease is poured down a sink. Viewers can see how liquid fat turns into a solid, sticky coating on the interior pipe walls, narrowing the channel and trapping debris. This visual directly reinforces the lesson that liquid grease does not stay liquid inside cold drain lines.
